summary: Kyle runs a fleet of AI coding agents daily across three machines: a MacBook for heavy coding, and two always-on headless Linux boxes (Linux A for long-running tasks, Linux B for short-lived side projects), all tied together by one control plane. His journey started with a single terminal and a few tmux panes, but he quickly became the human bottleneck — acting simultaneously as scheduler, memory, and reviewer across six live contexts. The key insight came from observing how executives run large companies: separate context per role. He built a real hierarchy of entity types (CEO, VP, manager, worker), each with scoped context and approval boundaries, so he only holds one top-level context instead of six. For state management, he moved agent state out of the model's context window into on-disk workspaces (mission, status, handoff folders), and replaced compaction with full resets — the agent clears context entirely and re-reads its own handoff files. A review gateway forces each layer to submit plans and block until approval, funneled into one web inbox. When scaling beyond one machine, five failures emerged: orchestrators doing work instead of delegating (fixed with CLI harness), pane overcrowding making tmux unreadable, OOM from stacked sessions, credential collisions across workspaces (fixed with separated environments), and laptop sleep/crash killing in-flight jobs (fixed with a boot command and offloading to Linux boxes). For cross-machine context transfer he uses Git commits and SSH tmux send-keys, with per-machine directories to avoid silent divergence. He collapsed multiple review gateways into one on an always-on Linux box, and adopted Discord as a single router with one bot per machine, making his phone the remote control. Four unsolved problems remain: consistency across machines, abstracting local-only tools, secure credential handoff, and resource management — all pointing toward a Kubernetes-style architecture where agents declare what they need, not where they run.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Fleet Overview and the Breaking Point
sections.summary: Kyle introduces his three-machine fleet (MacBook, Linux A, Linux B) as a real daily setup. He recounts starting with a single terminal and a few tmux panes, quickly escalating to six simultaneous contexts where he became the scheduler, memory, and reviewer — a human bottleneck that does not scale.

sections.title: Organizational Hierarchy and State Management
sections.summary: The unlock: model agents as an organization (CEO, VP, manager, worker), each a real entity type with scoped context and approval boundaries. State moves out of the context window into on-disk workspaces (mission, status, handoff). Instead of compacting, Kyle resets context entirely and lets the agent re-read its handoff files. A review gateway blocks layers until plan approval.

sections.title: Five Failures When Scaling Beyond One Machine
sections.summary: Five failures: (1) orchestrator doing work itself — fixed with CLI harness forcing delegation; (2) pane overcrowding making tmux unreadable; (3) OOM from stacked cloud code and MCP processes; (4) credential collisions — fixed with separated environments; (5) MacBook sleep/crash killing in-flight jobs — fixed with boot command and offloading to Linux boxes.

sections.title: Cross-Machine Solutions
sections.summary: Context transferred via Git commits and SSH tmux send-keys; per-machine directories prevent silent divergence. Multiple review gateways collapsed into one on always-on Linux. Discord adopted as single router with one bot per machine, making the phone a remote control for the fleet.

sections.title: Unsolved Problems and Kubernetes Convergence
sections.summary: Four unsolved problems: cross-machine consistency, local-only tools, secure credential handoff, and resource management. Kyle recognizes these map onto Kubernetes concepts (compute, secrets, tools, scheduling). He plans to stack Kubernetes underneath and build orchestration management on top, reusing what exists.

demonstrations: Live fleet running on one screen shown as a normal working session

limitations: Consistency across machines not yet solved
Local-only tools (MCP servers, browser) still stuck on the Mac
Secure credential handoff between instances unresolved
Resource management still manual — Kyle decides what runs where
Multi-machine orchestration is still rough and actively being built
